podcast.title: Inheritance and Persistence
podcast.body: Upon her mother's death in 1928, Florence inherited additional money, which she immediately reinvested into her singing career. She dismissed any laughter or criticism from others as mere jealousy, unwavering in her self-belief and commitment to her vocal pursuits. "When her mother died in 1928, she inherited even more money, which she then plowed right back into her singing career."

podcast.title: Mention in Outsider Music History
podcast.body: Florence Foster Jenkins is listed among artists previously covered as examples of outsider music, alongside Wesley Willis, The Shags, and others. "On those programs, I covered Wesley Willis, the Shags, the legendary Stardust cowboy, Jandic, Captain B. Fart, Daniel Johnson, Florence Foster Jenkins, and even Charles Manson."

podcast.title: Pioneering Outsider Recording Artist
podcast.body: Florence Foster Jenkins is identified as potentially the first outsider musician to have her work documented on record. She made several recordings between 1941 and 1944, which have since been reissued multiple times, including on CD and through iTunes, solidifying her historical significance in the realm of outsider art. "She made a number of recordings between 1941 and 1944, which have been reissued several times since then, including on CD and through iTunes, of course."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Singing Career Beginnings
podcast.body: Florence Foster Jenkins began her singing career with recitals in 1912, utilizing funds from an inheritance to support her artistic endeavors. She believed herself to be a brilliant opera singer, despite lacking a sense of rhythm, pitch, tone, or pacing, or any discernible musical talent. "She persisted using the funds from an inheritance to further her singing career, beginning with some recitals in 1912."
